537.k: **also** goes before the verb — also add (same as Idiomatic #21). "A bug that was missed" is a bug **that was missed** / a **missed** bug (*missing bug* means a bug that can't be found). Third person **uses**. "Not passing" is **without passing**. *drop it* is right (Idiomatic #20 deprecate correction applied).

538.k: "I don't understand what this says" casually is **I don't get what … is saying** / **I can't follow this comment**. "This can't be an issue at all" is **there's no way … could happen** (no need for *issue*; just *no way*). "Submitted before the form is complete" is **a half-filled / incomplete row gets submitted**. *the latest PR comment* article is right.

539.k: **the** default needs the article. Branches take **on** — on this branch (same as #2 stay **on** the branch). *set X as default* works; more idiomatic is **make X the default**.

541.k: **reply** is intransitive and needs **to** before its object — reply **to** the comment (same as Grammar · Verb & Object #5 reply me → reply to me, **second time**). To drop the preposition switch to a transitive verb: **answer the comment** / **address the comment** (same as #31); *respond to* also needs *to*. As a noun, **post a reply to X** is most common.

542.k: **need backend** isn't a noun phrase — *highlight* needs a noun: **the backend dependency**, or a clause **that this needs the backend (deployed first)**. "Flag for the reviewer" is **highlight / call out / flag** (*call out* is most casual). "In the PR" (the description body) is **in the PR**; a comment is *on* the PR (same as #11).

543.k: **if any pr match is incomplete** — *match* is transitive and needs an object, and here you mean "PRs with a backend dependency": say **whenever a PR has one / if a PR depends on backend work**. "Save as a rule" is **save this as a rule** or casually **remember this**. For rules **whenever** conveys "every time" better than *if*. Third-person singular **a PR has**.

544.k: Your sentence is correct. *look at* isn't wrong; to ask someone to check something casually **take a look at** is more common (or *check out*). (Original category: Idiomatic)

545.k: The verb *comment* takes **on** (comment on the ticket); with *add/post* it's a comment **to/on** the ticket. *yt* is fine casually; formally write YouTrack. (Original category: Prepositions & Articles)

546.k: *post* is transitive — post **it** (missing object, same as Grammar · Verb & Object). *yt* is casual; formally **YouTrack ticket** (same as #2).

547.k: "Then decide whether to…" uses **decide** (*address* means handling / responding to an issue or comment, same as Git #4 address the PR comment). **whether** takes an infinitive — whether **to post**, not *posting*. "Condensed version" is **a condensed version**.

548.k: *example* is countable and needs an article — **an** example **of** …. Don't stack long nouns (*Youtrack ticket content example* → an example of the ticket content). Spelling **YouTrack** (capital T).

549.k: **necessary + to + verb** (it's necessary **to append**; same infinitive rule as Grammar #18 better **to move**). *append* is transitive — **it**. **the** YouTrack ticket (spelling same as #3, #9). (Original category: Grammar)

550.k: The passive needs *be* + past participle — it**'s decided** by (*it decide* mixes active base form; same as Git #7 *is name*). "Up to someone" idiomatically: **that's ~'s call** / **it's up to ~**.

551.k: A specific list needs **the** (same as Git #3 update **the** PR). "On the ticket" is **on the ticket**.

552.k: The second listed countable noun also needs an article — a ticket and **a** branch. The product is spelled **YouTrack** (capital T, same as #5). *then do it* is very casual and natural. (Original category: Prepositions & Articles)

553.k: The verb is two words, **check out** (*checkout* is the noun; same as Git #2, **second time**). "Branch for a ticket" takes **for**; *with* means "together with the ticket". (Original category: Git)

554.k: The "range" of work is its **scope** (*range* is a numeric/date interval); *in the scope* takes **in**, not *to*. "Ticket content" is the ticket **description** (same as #10, now moved to leave series #18). Join two imperatives with **and** (comma splice, same as Git). (Original category: Idiomatic)

555.k: Make the conditional complete — **when/if the index is** … (*index=…* is code notation; in prose add *the … is*). A double possessive X's Y's Z is clunky — **the Z of Y inside X**. A ticket as a prefix: **For PROJ-101:**. (Original category: Grammar)

556.k: "A part of the ticket" is **the … section of** the ticket — hanging *part* right after the ticket number is Chinese order, and it needs **the** (document parts are usually **sections**; *part* is vaguer). "Change to the new spec" is **update X to match the new spec**, or **replace the old spec with the new one** (*replace* only takes *with*, same as "Could you" · replace). *take a look at* is right (#1 internalised). (Original category: Idiomatic)

557.k: Your sentence is grammatically correct; the lines below are more specific. The usual verbs for tickets are **open / file** a ticket/issue (*create* also works). Add the source so they don't guess — for the **Dependabot** vulnerabilities / the **dependency** vulnerabilities. The article in *a … issue* is right.

558.k: Another spot in the same repo is **the other place / component / call site** — *project* reads as a different project. **other** needs the (the known one). A singular relative-clause subject takes -s — **that uses** (*which use* is missing s; subject–verb agreement), and code descriptions usually use *that*, not *which*. "Open a ticket to track a to-do" can state the goal: **file an issue to switch X over to Y**. (Original category: Grammar)

559.k: Countable nouns need an article — the **title** (same as Prepositions #33, #34). To change title text use **change / update the title to**; **rename** leans toward files, variables, branches — things with identifiers. Put the new title in quotes so they know where it starts. (Original category: Prepositions & Articles)

560.k: A bare noun leaves them guessing the action — add a verb and preposition **put / save it in the X folder**. For "put it there instead" end with **instead**. A folder name as a proper noun takes no article, but the following *folder* needs **the**. (Original category: Grammar — missing verb)

561.k: "Replace" in everyday use is **replace**; in formal docs **supersede**. Add an object — **the … dashboard / page** — or *BI mdr-gen* reads like a code name. When the ticket number is the subject, natives often rephrase as **the new X from PROJ-101** so the sentence has a concrete subject. (Original category: Idiomatic)

10001.k: When turning a string of Chinese fragments into English, build full sentences: **turn X into Y** ("make the notes into a page"); 「歸類」 is **group … together**; 「代名詞」 here means stand-in names in code — **placeholders**. A *pronoun* is the grammar term (it / they).

10002.k: 「一律」 is **always** — put it first to sound like a rule; for a standing guideline, **X should always …** also works. 「暗黑背景」 is **a dark background / dark mode**; *black background* sounds too literal (pure black).

10003.k: 「會以為」 has no subject; English needs one — **it looks like … / people will think …**. 「不要出現」 is **don't use / avoid**, not *don't appear* (appear is intransitive; the thing itself must be the subject: *`Foo` shouldn't appear alongside `foo`*).

10004.k: *Correct* as an adjective means "right"; for "the phrasing you corrected" use the past participle — **corrected phrasing / your corrections**. When the subject is a thing, use the passive: **need to be saved** (*need to save* means the phrasing saves something). Add **in** before *this conversation*; you save **to** a page; capitalise **English**; ending with **too** sounds more natural than *also*.

10005.k: **could** is missing a verb — could X **be / work as** a name (could + noun straight into another noun isn't a sentence). "Represent any one feature" is **stand for / cover any feature**; *represent all the features* reads as representing every feature at once. The most idiomatic way to ask "is it general enough" is **Is X generic enough to …?**

10006.k: Ask "**how** to **translate**" with **How**, not **What** — *translate* already takes X as its object, so *what* has no slot (*what would you translate* asks "which thing would you translate"). To use *what*, say **What's the English for X?** Use one set of quotes, with the question mark outside.

10007.k: A specific section needs **the** — to **the** native-speaker section. **native part** is vague; say **the native-speaker section / the Native line**. Write **OK** in caps and start the instruction as a new sentence.

10008.k: A section takes **in**, not *at* — **in** the native-speaker section (*at* is for a point or position: at the top, at line 5). **the** key points needs the article (that entry's key points). The contraction **it's** sounds more natural than *it is*.

10009.k: **bold** works as a verb on its own — bold X; no need for *mark X bold* (*mark* leans toward tagging/ticking). You can also say **put X in bold**. A specific section needs **the**, and *native* alone isn't a noun — **the native-speaker lines / section** (same as Prepositions #103, #104). What's being bolded is a phrase (fold … into), so **key phrase** is more precise than *keyword*.

10010.k: The sentence is correct; only punctuation — the period inside the quotes doubles up with the question mark outside. **Drop the quoted period** and keep the question mark outside the quotes (what you're quoting isn't a question). Capitalise the quoted sentence: **Fold**.

10011.k: 「重新編號」 is **renumber** (a single verb). *renumber* is transitive — renumber **the entries** (missing object, same as Verb & Object). End the request with a question mark.

10012.k: A quoted phrase as a modifier still needs a noun after it — the "clean" **entries** together (same as "Could you" · group: the "get rid of" mistakes, quoted phrase before the noun). When listing options with slashes, add spaces — **clean / cleaner / cleanest** — so they read as three options.

10013.k: For bracketed labels **tags / notes** is more precise than *words*. "Do the same for every one" is **apply the same fix to every entry** — *fix it* sounds like repairing a bug; on this page each one is an **entry** (*item* suggests a list item).

10014.k: The linking words here are **connecting words / filler words** — *conjunctions* technically means grammatical joiners like and / but / or. "Not the important part" is **not the key point**. Splitting the two instructions into two sentences reads more clearly than one long *and* sentence.

10015.k: **when needs a full clause** — *when Search results* has no verb; use **In the search results, …** or **When I search, …** (same as the when-clause series). The words you typed are **the search terms**, and the usual verb for colouring them is **highlight**. **a** different colour needs the article; don't capitalise *search* mid-sentence.

10016.k: **move takes to for the destination** — move X **to** the end; *at the end* describes where something already is. Casually you can also say **put X last**. *Vue-specific* can go — the category is already called Vue.

10017.k: **this kind of "cleaner"** points at the word, but you mean the entries — **entries like …**. "clean / cleaner / cleanest" is a **series** inside Idiomatic Phrasing, not a category. Don't leave a stray space inside the quotes ("cleaner ").

10018.k: **in different is missing its noun** — in different **colours**. "Apply to the others" is **apply the same fix to** the others (*apply this issue* means applying the problem; same as Idiomatic #111). Write the ellipsis as **…** with spaces around it (pull … from).

10019.k: **with bullet is missing its noun and plural** — with these **bullet points** / a **bulleted list**. **mark the color "get"** doubles up the object; say **colour "get"** or **highlight "get" in the same colour**. *native* alone isn't a noun — **the native line** (same as Prepositions #103–105). Apply the same **to the other entries**.

10020.k: 「縮排」 is **indent**. The bullets are what gets indented, so use the passive **need to be indented** (same passive-voice issue). There are several, so use the plural **bullets**. The shortest version is the imperative **Indent the bullets.**

10021.k: **Embedded questions don't invert** — explain **what X is**, not *what is X* (same rule as the other embedded-question entries). Give both terms articles and full nouns — **a** gerund, **a transitive verb** (*transitive* is an adjective). Join the two with **and**; no stray spaces inside the quotes.

10022.k: A grammar term used as a noun needs an article or the plural — **the** infinitive / **infinitives** (same as the countable-noun article entries). To say what you're adding, use **a card for …**.

10023.k: **the** native-speaker lines needs the article and noun — *native* alone isn't a noun (same as Prepositions #103–105). Two full sentences joined by a comma is a comma splice; split them or use a dash. "The way I want to learn" is **the phrasing I want to learn**; *the native way* sounds like "the locals' customs".

10024.k: On this page each one is an **entry**; *item* suggests a list item (same as Idiomatic #111, **second time**). Make *this bug* clear — attach a screenshot or name the entry.

10025.k: Open an example with **For example, …** or **e.g.** — a lone *like* can read as "enjoy". Say what the problem is: **still isn't bold / still isn't highlighted**. After *native* add **the native-speaker line** (same as Prepositions #103–105, **fifth time**).

10026.k: "Just remove" is **remove X from Y** — *remove* takes **from**. Give *native* its noun: **the native-speaker lines** (same as Prepositions #103–105). Join the two quotes with **and**.

10027.k: **an input area that I can put something** is missing a preposition — for a place use **where** (= in which). "Input" is **type / enter**; *put* is too vague. The button is **the Send button**; *sending button* sounds off. After the when-clause, skip *you will* and use the imperative **replace it**.

10028.k: **would** is hypothetical; to describe the feature you want, use the present **suggest** or **so you can suggest**. "A better way to replace with" is simply **a better replacement** — the original dangles a preposition and adds an extra *the*. "Make it do B" is **have it + base verb** (see Infinitive · let / make / have).

10029.k: "* means any" is **a wildcard** / **\* matches anything** — *any* on its own is incomplete; say any **what** (any ticket number / any characters). Quote the field name and add **box** (the "text to replace" box). To describe the behaviour you want, use **treat it as …**.

10030.k: 「連動」 is **keep X in sync with Y** / **update X to match**. **something** is missing an e (*somthing*). After the if-clause, give the main action as an imperative: **update the search box**.

10031.k: A button needs *the* or just its name — **the Send button** / **Send**. 「直接取代」 is **replace it directly / just do the replacement**. 「而不是」 is **instead of + -ing** or **…, not …**. 「過濾條件」 is **a filter**.

10032.k: With *the box* as subject, the verb needs a modal — **should replace** (*box replace* is missing both -s and *should*). *replace all* should say all **what**: **every match / all occurrences**. Use **including the ones in …** for the scope.

10033.k: 「一模一樣」 here is **exactly as is / verbatim / as-is**. To state the rule, use the passive **should be inserted** (see Transitive verb · passive).

10034.k: **stylish** is an adjective ("fashionable"); the noun for 「樣式」 is **styling / formatting**. *Styling* is uncountable, so the verb is **is gone**. *bold* and *colour* as nouns need **the**.

10035.k: For "in case I don't want it", use **in case** or **so I can turn it off**; *if* reads as "add the switch only when I don't want it". The UI control is usually a **toggle**. **want X to act as Y** is more complete than *want X as Y*.

10036.k: 「切換開關」 is **flip / switch the toggle**. 「沒有重新過濾」 is **doesn't re-filter / doesn't update the results** — describe bug behaviour in the present tense.

10037.k: Add the noun **box** after the field name (same as the wildcard entry). Search output is usually plural — **the results are wrong**. When reporting, add **expected vs actual**: "I expected X, but got Y".

10038.k: With *the box* as a singular subject, use **needs** or **should** (same as the "box replace" entry). "Include the space" really means **match across spaces / span multiple words**. **a single word** is clearer than *one word*.

10039.k: For 「標記」 in a UI, say **highlight** (colour) or **bold**; *mark* is vague, so name the effect you want.

10040.k: Your sentence works. To be more specific, use the gerund **grouping … together** (a box **for** + -ing; see Gerund · after a preposition).

10041.k:
For natural language, 「解析」 is **interpret / parse**. 「並非完全等於」 is **not matched exactly / not an exact match**. Link cause and result with **so**.
Spot on — you've picked up the phrasing from the previous entry. Use double quotes "…" for the field name to match the earlier entries.

10043.k: Refer to a button by its label — **a Suggest button**. Adding it to a field takes **to** (add X **to** the box). Don't nest quotes "'…'".

10044.k: A chart or UI guide to colours is a **legend / colour key**. "Describe the meaning" is **explain what X means** (no inversion in embedded questions). *A meaning description* is a literal translation.

10045.k: "On the left side" is **on the left** (*at the left* is less common). *which below* is missing its verb (*which **is** below*), but a plain prepositional phrase **below …** is tighter. The left column is usually **the sidebar**.

10046.k: Works as a note, but a full sentence needs a verb — **Use yellow for …** / **Make X yellow**. Ordinals take **the** (the first).

10047.k: It's **replace A with B** — *replace* doesn't take *to* (see the replace series). Or use **change A to B**. Before a singular countable noun, use **another**, not *other*.

10048.k: For exchanging two things, **swap** is the usual verb (*switch* also works). Add **the** before the ordinals, and make it plural — **colours**.

10049.k: **add needs a noun** — add **an option to** search … (*add search* is missing the thing being added). *native* alone isn't a noun — **the native-speaker lines** (same as Prepositions #103–105, #108 — **fifth time**). "Narrow the search to" is **limit the search to X**.

10050.k: "No you / me / I" is usually called an **impersonal style** (strictly it's impersonal, not third person). Three ways to rewrite: **imperative** (Could you merge … → **Merge …**), **passive** (Should we rename X → **Should X be renamed**), and **noun-style notes** (I tested it → **Tested:** …). "Put it first" is **put it first**.

10051.k: Name a button by its label — **a Renumber button**. "No need to … anymore" is **no longer needs to be …** (impersonal passive) or **stop + -ing**.
